evidence.claim: Sugar Camp combines 20 miles of paved highway with eight miles of maintained gravel on a 28-mile drive.
evidence.quote: Travel on this 28-mile drive, which combines 20 miles of paved highway and a nice 8-mile section of national forest scenic byway on maintained gravel-road.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service presents this National Forest Scenic Byway as a winding route through wooded hills and valleys, with vistas of distant landscapes.
evidence.quote: Most of the route is along wooded hills and valleys, which are covered with mixed hardwoods, intermingled with eastern red cedar and pine stands. Vistas provide the opportunity to view distant landscapes.

evidence.claim: Mixed hardwoods share the hills with eastern red cedar and pine.
evidence.quote: covered with mixed hardwoods, intermingled with eastern red cedar and pine stands.

evidence.claim: Settlers tapped sugar maples here for sap.
evidence.quote: Among the varied trees are sugar maples, which settlers used to tap for their sap (maple syrup) in years gone by.

evidence.claim: Another chapter of forest work left a more conspicuous structure: the Civilian Conservation Corps built Sugar Camp Fire Tower in the 1930s.
evidence.quote: Sugar Camp Fire Tower, built by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) in the 1930s.

evidence.claim: From Highway 112 south of Roaring River State Park, the route turns onto Forest Road 197.
evidence.quote: From Highway 112 just south of Roaring River State Park travel south approximately 2 miles, turn left onto Forest Road 197

evidence.claim: The gravel reaches Highway 86 near Table Rock Lake, and the remaining drive winds through forest toward the Cassville area.
evidence.quote: The gravel road eventually returns to civilization where it meets Highway 86 near Table Rock Lake. The remainder of the route winds through more swaths of forest before returning you to the Cassville area.

evidence.claim: A medicine-show fortune helped create Roaring River State Park.
evidence.quote: Land for the park was originally donated by Thomas Mark “Doc” Sayman, a medicine-show man who made millions peddling patent medicines and soaps during his traveling tent shows in the early 20th century.

evidence.claim: Thomas Mark “Doc” Sayman bought 2,400 acres and gave them to the state after failing to persuade the game and fish commission to purchase the spring property.
evidence.quote: When Sayman failed to get the game and fish commission to buy property at Roaring River Spring, he purchased 2,400 acres which he then turned over to the state.

evidence.claim: The park was acquired in 1923, then developed by the Civilian Conservation Corps and Works Progress Administration between 1933 and 1939.
evidence.quote: The original park was acquired in 1923, and developed between 1933 and 1939 by the Civilian Conservation Corps and Works Progress Administration.

evidence.claim: The CCC rebuilt an earlier mill dam for the fish hatchery in 1933.
evidence.quote: The dam was reconstructed by the CCC in 1933 for an important fish hatchery complex.

evidence.claim: Its Deer Leap Trail has rough stone steps, retaining walls and an overlook.
